summary: This Standards Track document specifies the "Incremental" HTTP header field, which tells HTTP intermediaries to forward the message incrementally.

plainLanguage.summary: A note on a package that says: pass it along as pieces arrive and do not wait for it all.

questions: what is the incremental http header
how to stop proxies buffering http responses
what does incremental true value mean
subtitle: A header that asks proxies and other HTTP intermediaries to pass a message along as it arrives instead of buffering it.

tldr.problem: HTTP intermediaries are allowed, and often deployed, to buffer a whole message before forwarding it. That breaks applications that rely on data arriving piece by piece, such as Server-Sent Events.
tldr.mechanism: The sender adds an Incremental header field with the value ?1. Intermediaries that understand it SHOULD NOT buffer the whole message and instead forward the content bytes as they arrive, or answer with an error.
tldr.outcome: It is only a request: intermediaries that do not know the field keep buffering, so clients that depend on it need prior knowledge or must probe for support.

today: RFC 10036 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2026, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It relies on RFC 9110 for HTTP semantics and on RFC 9209 for the Proxy-Status field.

sections.title: Why Buffering Causes Trouble
sections.content:
HTTP lets a receiver start working on part of a message as it arrives. Some applications are built on that. Server-Sent Events uses one long-running response in which the server keeps sending notifications. With Chunked Oblivious HTTP Messages, a client opens a request and sends data bit by bit while the server can start answering before the request is complete, so the pair acts like a two-way channel.

Intermediaries are the problem. They are permitted, and frequently deployed, to buffer a complete message before forwarding it. An intermediary that waits for a never-ending event stream could wait indefinitely, and the client might never receive any part of the response. In a two-way exchange, buffering whole requests or responses prevents any data from being delivered.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a mail clerk who waits until a whole story has been written before passing on the first page. If the story never ends, you never get a page. This note asks the clerk to pass pages along right away.

sections.title: The Incremental Header Field
sections.content:
The Incremental header field is a structured field of type Item, and only Boolean values are valid. A recipient ignores the field if it holds any other type.

  • Incremental: ?1 asks intermediaries to forward the message incrementally.
  • Incremental: ?0 means the default behavior from HTTP, where intermediaries might buffer the entire message. The explicit signal might give an intermediary more confidence in choosing to buffer.

The field applies to each HTTP message. If both the request and the response need incremental forwarding, the field MUST be set on both. The document defines no parameters, but future documents might, and receivers MUST ignore unknown parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has two settings: a yes (pass it along as it comes) and a no (wait if you like). If you want it both ways, there, and back, you must put a note on the package going out and on the one coming back.

sections.title: What Intermediaries Should Do
sections.content:
On seeing a header section with a true Incremental value, an intermediary SHOULD NOT buffer the entire message. It SHOULD send the header section downstream and keep forwarding the content bytes as they arrive. Because the field is only about message content, an intermediary can still buffer the whole header section and trailer section.

If an intermediary decides outright to refuse incremental forwarding, it MUST generate an error response rather than buffering the whole message. HTTP implementations whose APIs cannot transfer content incrementally SHOULD use the field to reduce or disable buffering.

Support is not guaranteed. Intermediaries that are unaware of the field will not change behavior, so clients that depend on incremental forwarding can rely on prior knowledge or probe for support on individual resources.
sections.plainLanguage: If the clerk sees the note, they should pass pieces on as they come. If they truly cannot, they must say so loudly instead of quietly sitting on the package.

sections.title: Bidirectional Channels Over HTTP
sections.content:
Setting the field on both a request and its response asks intermediaries to forward early responses and to send content incrementally in both directions. That helps establish a bidirectional byte channel over HTTP.

The RFC adds a caution: when designing bidirectional protocols over HTTP, Extended CONNECT is generally more consistent with HTTP's architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: If both the question and the answer carry the note, both sides can talk while the other is still talking, like a phone call made of mail. The RFC says a real phone line (Extended CONNECT) often fits HTTP better.

sections.title: Refusing: Error Responses
sections.content:
An intermediary that understands the field might still reject a request for security reasons. Two cases are described.

Permanent rejection. Some intermediaries inspect message content and forward it only if it looks safe, which needs the entire message. If such an intermediary cannot forward incrementally because of security concerns about the content, it SHOULD respond with a 501 (Not Implemented) error carrying the incremental_refused Proxy-Status response header field.

Temporary rejection. Intermediaries often limit concurrent requests and buffer those over the limit. They could apply a stricter limit to incremental requests so capacity remains for other requests. When rejecting because that limit is reached, they SHOULD respond with 429 (Too Many Requests) and a connection_limit_reached Proxy-Status field.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk may say "not allowed, I need to check the whole package" (501) or "too many open packages right now, try later" (429).

sections.title: Small Packets and Buffer Limits
sections.content:
Intermediaries might use a small amount of buffering even for incremental messages, for performance and efficiency. Forwarding everything immediately could be exploited to make an intermediary waste effort on many small packets. An intermediary might therefore limit the number of bytes buffered or the time buffers are held.

Any buffering can hurt application latency, even when it improves efficiency. In all cases data cannot be held indefinitely and needs to be forwarded when either the time limit or the byte limit is reached.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk can gather a few tiny pieces into one trip so they are not run back and forth for every crumb, but they cannot hold them forever.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The document registers an HTTP field named Incremental in the HTTP Field Name Registry, with status permanent and structured type Item. It also registers the proxy error type incremental_refused in the HTTP Proxy Error Types registry, with recommended HTTP status code 501, generated only by intermediaries.
sections.plainLanguage: The new note and the new "I refuse" stamp are both written into official lists so everyone uses the same names.
